Richard O'Neill, Silver Spring, MD.
An ISO Process for Holding Existing Consumers Harmless from New Large Consumers
Richard ONeill
September 2026

On September 15, 2026, the House passed a bill to require states to consider taking up standards that would force tech companies to shoulder the electricity cost increases associated with large data centers. The bill doesn’t actually require them to regulate. This type of ‘to consider’ law generally indicates that a stronger bill did not have the votes. On the same day, the House passed a bill for FERC to establish regional joint boards to study electric load forecasting and report to Congress only a slightly higher than ‘to consider’. The Senate acted on neither. New data centers are currently opposed by a super majority of the population, because they believed to raise electricity prices, consume water for cooling, are noisy, are very secret about their intentions, and cause job losses. Below is something to consider.   

Covert Operations.  One of the ongoing issues is that NCLs are generally very secretive about their intentions. The following story is an example.  In Arkansas, the issue was whether Google will pay the full cost of a new power plant that will serve a data center, which it has said it will do. The ARPSC mistakenly released documents related to the contract between Google and Entergy. Newspapers published stories describing the information they contain. Entergy claimed the papers published inaccurate (possibly fake) information and sought a restraining order to block dissemination of the leak. On Sept. 2, 2026, federal Judge Lee Rudofsky denied the request for a temporary restraining order and said: “Public utility companies’ special arrangements with a large data center may very well have repercussions across the state, presumably, or at least potentially, in both very positive and potentially, or presumably, negative ways”. On September 16, 2026, Entergy Arkansas voluntarily dismissed its lawsuit (Arkansas Business). Surprising ECs with a data center ‘Xmas present’ is like putting coal in their stocking. IPPs should not be forced into hedges with ECs.

Special Rates. For over a century, vertically integrated utilities have been offering special rates (prices) to large consumers with state approval, for example, industrial consumers who would bring jobs to the state or if there was excess capacity. Currently, data centers do not seem to fit this model.  For existing consumers, Bring Your Own Generation (and Transmission) (BYOG) for new large consumers (NLCs) does not necessarily keep existing consumers (ECs) from paying more for electricity. For example, if the data center brings more expensive generation, it will probably not hold existing consumer harmless (HECH) in the current ISO markets.  If the NCLs bring gas powered generation to the market, increasing demand for natural gas will, most likely, raise the costs to all gas generators. Unless stated otherwise, we assume that NCLs either bring less efficient generation to market or do not bring enough generation to market. If an NCL brings more efficient generation to cover the NCL’s consumption, the NCL holds ECs harmless. There is no perfect way to hold harmless, but you can come close.

Generation. Generation costs come in three flavors: fixed and sunk, fixed but avoidable if not dispatched, and marginal. Increasing the demand for new generation increases the sunk cost of new generation. Currently, there is a backlog of orders for some generation and transmission equipment and not surprisingly the prices have increased. Increasing gas-fired generation may need additional pipeline investment. In 1999, FERC changed to ‘hold harmless’ for new gas pipeline investment. Additional transmission investment needed for NCLs should be paid for by the NLCs and they should receive flowgate rights. Vertical integration is not the answer. ISO markets have proved to be much more efficient and reliable. 

Hedging. Hedging is a risk management tool to stabilize prices. It is too late to find a low price hedge when the expectation is for higher prices. Risk management comes in two different flavors: reliability and energy prices. Reliability is a system-level ISO problem. Energy prices are an individual entity’s problem. Hedging is mostly a function of the balance sheet. 

IPPs are under no obligation to provide generous hedges. States are partially hedged by IOUs they regulate. On a nationwide basis, IPPs account for ~48% of total net generation (~2 trillion kWh), IOUs account for ~38%, Co-ops account for ~5% and Publicly/Federally Owned Utilities account for ~8% (EIA).

ISO filings. Today, ISO market rules and proposals appear to raise prices to existing customers (ECs). Curtailing new large consumers (NLCs), when the system is stressed is not enough. In unstressed periods, increased consumption from the new NLCs will raise the prices to all.  The existing consumers are not protected in non-stressed periods, which is currently most of the time. The basic assumption is the increased consumption increases clearing prices. There are instances where this may not be true, for example, the data center brings only PV and battery storage or there is just a little more consumption to take advantage of scale economies of a generator not at capacity. Generators at capacity have exhausted scale economies. 

Consumers. The consumer side of ISO markets are controlled by the state (~70%) and is neck-deep in the old cost-of-service regime. Paying consumers not to consume (aka DR) is difficult to measure, robbing Peter to pay Paul, distorts price signals, and is a moral hazard. State governance of retail prices can distort the transmission level energy prices.  It is time to put large consumers into the ISO market for reliability (NLCs are a potential reliability problem) and efficiency. NLCs could subsidize rooftop solar. Elon promised us solar roofs several years ago. Currently, solar roofs are significantly more expensive than traditional rack-mounted panels paired with an asphalt roof and have lower energy efficiency. Below is a method to hold existing consumers harmless, that is, energy at a price without NCLs. 

Capacity Markets. Capacity markets have a bad pedigree and exist to ‘guarantee’ that inflexible demand is served.  When all else fails, we ask consumers to turn their lights to ‘keep the lights on’. Capacity markets should be rethought. They are a bad solution to the ‘missing money’ problem in the energy markets, not as granular as energy markets, necessary because ECs do not bid into the energy market, and distort the interconnection and transmission expansion problem.

The ISO energy prices are and have been too low since inception. Consequently, they raise and distort capacity and investment prices. Unlike other energy pricings methods currently in use, AIC pricing eliminates makewhole payments and sends a better price signals. It is not much different from convex hull pricing, but with less computation no makewhole payments, and uplift payments. Consumer bidding should the set scarcity prices and if bids are flexible enough, should not pay capacity prices. States need to play a greater role in resource adequacy (RA).

Transmission. Firm and interruptible transmission is a construct from vertically integrated utilities and should not exist in ISOs. NRIS service is expensive and exists to allow generators access to the capacity market.  In ISO energy markets, the idea of firm and interpretable transmission rights and economic dispatch are fundamentally incompatible. This issue stems from the poor modeling of capacity expansion and weak implementation of beneficiaries pay.  Each ISO has its own approach. We have gone down the rabbit hole. 

Behind the meter generation. If all generation is ‘behind the meter’ and there is no gas generation, the data center can sell its excess into the ISO market lowering the price. This comes close to hold harmless. Buying from the market mostly violates HECH. The data center can be an island. (Libertarians usually choose islands. They put little value on reliability and overall market efficiency.) 

Beyond the meter generation. A simple and relatively easy way to implement a HECH solution is first to run the day-ahead market with all consumers and generators. This establishes the economic dispatch for all consumers and generators that optimizes market surplus. In addition, it establishes the prices for generators and a price signal for entry and exit.  After that remove all NCLs and run a HECH day-ahead market. This establishes the prices for ECs that holds them harmless.  The existing consumers pay the ‘hold harmless’ market clearing price with the first day-ahead market dispatch. To achieve revenue neutrality (RN), the NCLs pay the difference revenues from the ECs and the payment to generators. 

All generators and consumers are fully hedged in the real-time market from the first day-ahead market dispatch.  In non-convex markets, there are no guarantees for this process, but with high probability, the existing consumers are held harmless.    

Notation 
EC	Existing Market Participant  
NLC	New Large Consumer (for example, large data centers) 
pECs + NCLs	First day-ahead market dispatch vector
λECs + NCLs	First day-ahead market clearing price vector 
λECs 	HECH day-ahead market clearing price vector 
A	Is the cost to existing consumers with all generators or existing generators before NLCs
A+B+C+D	Is the cost to all consumers under efficient dispatch
B+C+D	Payment from NCLs
